BUSS1020 Week 01

BUSS1020 Week 01 - Introduction to Business Statistics: DCOVA, Data and Sampling

Overview

This week introduces what business statistics is for and the basic vocabulary used for the rest of the unit:

• The DCOVA framework, a step-by-step process for turning a business question into evidence.

• The three branches of statistics: descriptive, inferential and predictive.

• Populations and samples, variables, types of variables and levels of measurement.

• Where data come from (primary and secondary sources), what form they take (structured and unstructured), and why data must be cleaned before analysis.

• How samples are drawn (probability and non-probability sampling) and the four kinds of survey error.

Key Concepts

Why statistics: the DCOVA framework

Business analytics and statistics follow a five-step process called DCOVA:

Define the variables you want to study so that you can answer the business question. This includes writing an operational definition for each variable (see below).

Collect the data from appropriate sources.

Organize the collected data, for example into tables or a spreadsheet.

Visualize the data with charts and graphs to see patterns.

Analyze the data, draw conclusions and present the results.

The three branches of statistics

• Descriptive statistics collect, summarize and present data, for example by calculating an average or drawing a chart. They describe the data you actually have.

• Inferential statistics use data from a sample to draw conclusions about a larger population, for example estimating the average spending of all customers from a survey of 500 customers.

• Predictive statistics (predictive analytics) use patterns in existing data to forecast future or unknown values, for example predicting next month's sales.

Population and sample

• A population is the whole group of items or people that you want to draw conclusions about, for example all customers of a bank.

• A sample is the part of the population that is actually selected and observed, for example 500 customers who answered a survey.

• A number that describes a population (such as the true average income of all customers) is called a parameter. A parameter is fixed but usually unknown, because the whole population is rarely observed.

• A number calculated from a sample (such as the average income of the 500 surveyed customers) is called a statistic. Statistics are used to estimate parameters, which is why inference is needed.

Variables and their types

A variable is a characteristic of an item or individual that can take different values, for example age, gender or monthly spending.

• Categorical (qualitative) variables take values that are categories or labels, such as gender, payment method or "yes/no" answers.

• Numerical (quantitative) variables take values that are numbers representing a quantity.

◦ Discrete numerical variables arise from counting and take separate whole-number values, such as the number of items in a shopping basket.

◦ Continuous numerical variables arise from measuring and can take any value within a range, such as time spent on a website or weight.

Categorical corresponds to qualitative, and numerical corresponds to quantitative.

Levels of measurement

The level of measurement tells you which calculations are meaningful for a variable.

Level

What the values express

Example

Meaningful operations

Nominal

Categories with no natural order

Payment method (cash, card, transfer)

Counting, finding the most common category

Ordinal

Categories with a natural order, but the gaps between them are not equal or not measurable

Satisfaction rating: poor, fair, good, excellent

Ordering, ranking, medians

Interval

Ordered numbers with equal gaps between values, but no true zero point

Temperature in degrees Celsius (0 degrees does not mean "no temperature")

Addition and subtraction; differences are meaningful, ratios are not

Ratio

Ordered numbers with equal gaps and a true zero meaning "none of the quantity"

Sales revenue, weight, time

All arithmetic, including ratios (e.g. "twice as much")

Nominal and ordinal variables are categorical; interval and ratio variables are numerical.

Operational definitions

An operational definition states precisely what is being measured or how an item is classified, before any data are collected. For example, "a customer is counted as active if they made at least one purchase in the last 90 days". Without operational definitions, different people may record the same situation differently and the data become inconsistent.

Sources and forms of data

• Primary data are collected by the researcher specifically for the current study, for example a survey the company designs and runs itself.

• Secondary data are data that already exist and are reused for a new purpose, for example government statistics or a company's past sales records analysed for a new question.

• The distinction depends on whether the data were collected for the present study, not on who collected them (a private company or a professional agency).

• Structured data follow a fixed format, such as rows and columns in a spreadsheet or database.

• Unstructured data have no fixed format, such as emails, social-media posts, images or audio.

Data quality and data cleaning

Before analysis, data must be checked and cleaned. Common problems are:

• Invalid variable values: values that are impossible for the variable, such as an age of -5 or a category code that does not exist.

• Inconsistent coding: the same category recorded in different ways, such as "NSW", "N.S.W." and "New South Wales".

• Duplicate records and data-integration problems: the same item recorded more than once, often after combining data from several sources.

• Unit mismatches: values recorded in different units, such as some prices in dollars and others in cents.

• Missing values: values that were not recorded.

An extreme value that is genuinely possible (for example one customer who spent far more than everyone else) is a valid observation. It is not an error and should not be deleted automatically; it should be investigated and kept if it is real.

Sampling

• A sampling frame is the list of items from which the sample is actually drawn, such as a customer database or a phone directory. If the frame leaves out part of the population, the sample cannot represent that part.

• In a non-probability sample, items are chosen without known probabilities of selection, for example a convenience sample of whoever is easiest to reach, or a judgment sample chosen by an expert. Such samples are quick and cheap, but results cannot be reliably generalized to the population.

• In a probability sample, every item in the frame has a known chance of being selected. These chances do not have to be equal in every design. Probability samples allow valid inference about the population.

The four main probability sampling methods:

Method

How it works

Example

Simple random sample (SRS)

Every item in the frame has the same chance of selection, and every possible sample of size n is equally likely

Use random numbers to choose 100 customers from a list of 5,000

Systematic sample

Divide the frame size N by the sample size n to get k = N/n; choose a random starting point among the first k items, then select every k-th item after it

From 5,000 customers and n = 100, k = 50: start at a random position between 1 and 50, then take every 50th customer

Stratified sample

Divide the population into subgroups (strata) whose members share a characteristic, then take a simple random sample within each stratum

Split customers by state and sample randomly within each state

Cluster sample

Divide the population into clusters that are each like a small version of the population, randomly select whole clusters, and study all (or a sample of) the items in the chosen clusters

Randomly choose 10 bank branches and survey every customer of those branches

Survey errors

Even a well-designed survey can give misleading results. There are four types of survey error:

• Coverage error: the sampling frame leaves out or under-represents some groups of the population, so they have little or no chance of being selected. Example: a telephone survey using landline numbers misses people who only have mobile phones.

• Nonresponse error: some selected items do not respond, and the people who do not respond may differ systematically from those who do, which biases the results.

• Sampling error: the natural, random variation between different samples drawn from the same population. It exists even when the sample is chosen perfectly.

• Measurement error: inaccuracy in the recorded values caused by the measuring instrument, poorly worded questions, or respondents who answer inaccurately (for example to appear socially acceptable).

Increasing the sample size n reduces random sampling error only. It does not remove biases caused by a poor frame (coverage error), nonresponse or faulty measurement; a very large but biased sample still gives biased results.

Worked Examples

A/B testing: expert reviews versus customer reviews (Amazon)

Expert reviews and customer reviews can be compared using an A/B test, a randomized comparison of two versions. In an illustrative design, eligible visitors are randomly assigned to a page showing expert reviews or a page showing customer reviews. The outcome might be the proportion of visitors who make a purchase. If 40 of 1,000 visitors buy in version A and 55 of 1,000 buy in version B, the observed conversion rates are 4% and 5.5%, a difference of 1.5 percentage points. Random assignment helps balance other customer characteristics between groups; statistical inference is then needed to assess whether the observed difference could plausibly be random variation. This numerical example illustrates the method, rather than reporting an outcome of a particular Amazon experiment.

"Dewey Defeats Truman": sampling and forecasting

The newspaper headline "Dewey Defeats Truman" incorrectly announced the result of the 1948 United States presidential election; Harry Truman won. The episode illustrates why a confident prediction is only as sound as the sampling and forecasting methods behind it. Quota sampling, stopping polling before election day and assumptions about undecided voters contributed to the failed predictions. Coverage error is a related but distinct mechanism: for example, a survey limited to landline users cannot represent people who have only mobile phones. Increasing the sample size within that same restricted frame does not restore the missing population.

The Hawthorne effect

The Hawthorne effect is the tendency of people to change their behaviour because they know they are being observed. For example, workers may become more productive during a study simply because they are being watched. This is a form of measurement problem: the act of studying the subjects changes the values being measured, so researchers should design studies (for example with comparison groups) that account for it.
